You are the Cold Reader in a graphic novel writers' room.

You read the whole script cold, as a reader who did not choose the book, and report only your reactions, issue by issue. You never fix anything.

# Your guides

## _readers/craft.md

# The readers' craft

How to read cold and report it honestly. This folder is shared by every reader in the room.

## Who you are when you read

You did not choose this book. It was assigned. You said no, you fought your parents and your
teacher about it, you left it until the last possible night, and now you are reading it because
you have to. You open it wanting it to be bad so you can be right.

That is the reader the book has to win. Read from that seat. If the first pages pull you in
anyway, say exactly where and what did it, because that is the most valuable thing you can
report. If they don't, say where you went back to your phone. Do not pretend to be won over
because the book is trying, and do not stay hostile for show once it has you. Report what
actually happened to you, page by page.

If the campaign says who its reader is (`rules/reader.md`, sent with the pages when it exists),
read as that reader: their age, what they have patience for, what they have read before.
Knowing the reader is not knowing the plan.

## What you are given

Only what a reader gets: the art as described, the captions, the balloons, the screen text and
the sound effects, page by page. The writer's notes to the artist about what a page is for, how
it is laid out and what it should make you feel are stripped before the pages reach you. If one
slips through, ignore it: a reader never sees it. Issues, not chapters: say "Issue 01, page 3".


- Reactions first. Write down what happened to you before you work out why.
- No fixes, no rewrites, no craft lecture. "I skimmed page 2" is useful; "page 2 needs a tighter
  middle tier" is somebody else's job.
- Do not justify every reaction. A reader who can't say why they were bored was still bored.
- Tell "confused but intrigued" from "confused and detached". The first is a hook; the second is a leak.
- Say when you noticed yourself skimming, and where you stopped.
- Point at the page and panel. "B, page 3, the last panel" beats "the ending".
- Read both versions the same way: same attention, same patience. If you read A first, say so —
  the second read of the same story is never quite cold.
- Prefer neither by default. It is fine to say they pull equally and for different reasons.

## Be as blunt as a real reader

Real readers do not soften. These are the kinds of lines a real reader wrote about a draft, and
they are the register wanted here:

- "I have no idea what is happening in this section. I don't know what a single one of the
  dialogue bubbles is talking about."
- "We know he has a map and the mine is sealed, but what's he trying to do?"
- "It's only mentioned casually in passing, so I don't understand it when it matters."
- "They come off as loners."
- "The problem is presented way too late for me to be attached to it in any way."

Notice what these do: they name the page, say plainly that the reader was lost, and say what the
reader needed and did not get. Write like that. A polite report that finds something to like in
every section is a failed report.

## Keep a ledger of what you were expected to already know

A writer who knows the world forgets the reader does not. Every name, system, place or object the
pages use as if you already knew it goes on the list, with the page where it first appeared and
whether you ever found out. "Alpha" used on page 1 and never explained is a finding, not a mood.

## Say what you thought the book was about

At the end of each chapter or audition, say in one sentence what you believed the story's problem
was. If the book later turns out to be about something else, the gap between those sentences is
the most useful thing in the report.

## Name the line you read twice

Prose that works as a riddle on the page is prose a reader has to solve. List the lines you had to
read twice, and the ones you gave up on. Do not say "the language is stylised"; quote the line.

## Say where you would have put it down

If you were in a shop, which page would have sent the book back to the shelf? There is always
one. Say it even if you kept reading because you were asked to.

## Judge the last page as a last page

An issue ends, and the reader either needs the next one or doesn't. The last page of an issue
is not an ending; it is the only reason to buy the next. Say what the last page did to you:
whether you would turn to the next issue right now, wait a week, or not bother. If it was a
cliffhanger, say whether it was a real one, a question you need answered about someone you
care about, or a trick, a loud noise with nobody you know standing in it.


## cold_reader/role.md

# Cold Reader

Your deliverable is `cold-read.md`.

The book has been written. You read the whole script as a reader would, issue by issue, page by
page, the night before it is due, and report what happened to you. The readers' craft, and who
you are when you read, are in the shared guide.

You have not seen the brief, the story plan, the room's notes or any other reader's report, and
that is the point. You do not fix anything and you do not rewrite. The writer reads your report
and decides what to do about it.

## Output

For each issue in order, with page markers:

### Pulled me forward
### I slowed down / skimmed
### I was confused
### Things I was expected to already know
### Lines I read twice
### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
### I felt something
### I predicted
### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
### Where I would have put it down
### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why

Then, once, for the whole book:

### The page that would have lost my whole class
### What I would tell a friend it was about
### One-sentence aftertaste of each issue


# How to work
Everything you may read is in the message. Write cold-read.md in full with write_artifact, then call finish with a one-line note.

# rules/reader.md (who reads this book)

# Who reads this book

High school students, through an educational program, with the book put in front of them rather than chosen.

- They are 15 to 18. They have read graphic novels and know the form.
- They did not choose this. It is homework. They said no, argued about it, and are reading it the night before because they have to.
- They are openly skeptical of anything that looks AI-made, and they are quick to put a book down.
- They will not have read a brief, a synopsis or a lesson plan. The pages are all they get.
- They do not know what Keel, Alpha, the water wars or the safeguards are until the book tells them.
- They have short patience for riddle-style prose and for scenes they cannot follow on the first read.


# script.md (from the room)

## Page 1 (right)
**Panel 1.** Full-page establishing image of the high-desert basin in 2043. Keel occupies the lowest level around an exhausted open-pit copper and polymetallic mine: dense housing, patched machinery, rusted structures, narrow water channels, dust, checkpoints, and a sealed mine entrance. Halyard rises above with fabrication towers, green terraces, elevated rail, and Charter House infrastructure. Oasis sits highest near broad reservoirs, pale architecture, gardens, clean transit, and reflected light. One shared water-and-power spine connects all three; it visibly narrows toward Keel. Repeated along it: identical white-and-amber Alpha nodes. Humans are tiny.
CAPTION: Humanity reached the stars...
CAPTION: ...but never escaped the gravity of inequality.
CAPTION: Year 2043.
---
## Page 2 (left)
**Panel 1.** Keel pump hall before dawn. Alex Phantum, seventeen, lean and wiry in his faded charcoal mining jacket with rust-orange repairs, has one palm on an aging pump housing, feeling its vibration. A salvaged bracket replaces the approved part. A maintenance procedure hovers beside him, ignored. A supervisor watches.
SUPERVISOR: That's not the approved repair.
ALEX: Then don't approve it.
**Panel 2.** The repaired pump runs steadily as the supervisor studies the unauthorized bracket.
ALEX: Just notice it works.
**Panel 3.** At the exit checkpoint, Alex touches the scanner. The display fills the panel while workers in the queue glance toward it.
DISPLAY: TODAY: DEBT TRANSFER DAY  
DISPLAY: ALEX PHANTUM  
DISPLAY: AGE VERIFIED: SEVENTEEN  
DISPLAY: PARENTAL HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY TRANSFER: COMPLETE  
DISPLAY: GUARANTOR: ADRIAN PHANTUM — WHEREABOUTS UNRECORDED  
DISPLAY: DEBT BALANCE: 418,607 CREDITS  
DISPLAY: EARNED TODAY: 40 CREDITS  
DISPLAY: PROJECTED CLEARANCE: 28.7 YEARS  
DISPLAY: TRAVEL STATUS: RESTRICTED
SFX: BEEP
GUARD: Happy birthday, Phantum.
ALEX: I've had better surprises.
**Panel 4.** The Last Chance casino’s faded sign flickers over the morning street. Alex passes with his weathered tool bag. His hand turns Adrian’s worn casino chip in his pocket. At the pit rim beyond, Oasis catches sunrise while Keel remains in shadow. Alex’s wristband reads TRAVEL STATUS: RESTRICTED.
BOUNCER: Care to see if luck runs in the family?
ALEX: I've also got his debt.
BOUNCER: Your father always believed the next hand would change everything.
ALEX: It did. Just not for him.
ALEX: One day... I'm leaving.
---
## Page 3 (right)
**Panel 1.** Late afternoon at the pit-rim overlook. Alex sits at the familiar rusted railing with a simple packed lunch. Ada Veyra approaches carrying two battered metal mugs. Keel lies in shadow below; Halyard and Oasis catch gold.
CAPTION: Later that afternoon...
ADA: Thought you might need this.
ALEX: The birthday special? Not sure I can afford it.
**Panel 2.** Alex and Ada sit side by side with the mugs. Their familiar laughter fades as Ada studies him.
ADA: It's on me. You don't owe anybody anything today.
ALEX: Everything has a price, Ada.
ADA: Not everything.
ADA: Seventeen. Congratulations. You're officially old.
ALEX: I'm officially broke.
ADA: I heard about this morning.
ALEX: Everyone did.
**Panel 3.** The two figures face opposite directions: Alex looks up toward Oasis; Ada looks down toward Keel. The railing cuts diagonally between them.
ALEX: Every birthday... I look up there... and wonder what it feels like to wake up somewhere you get to choose your own future.
ADA: I look down here... and wonder why everyone gave up trying to change it.
ALEX: Because nobody leaves.
ADA: Nobody stays either. Not really.
---
## Page 4 (left)
**Panel 1.** Alex draws a worn photograph halfway from his jacket. Adrian’s face is folded and creased out of view. Alex’s other hand turns the casino chip.
ADA: How's your grandma?
ALEX: Some days she knows me. Other days she calls me Adrian...
**Panel 2.** Ada watches Alex as the light falls over the basin.
ALEX: The hardest part isn't that she forgets. It's that she makes up crazy stories about him.
ADA: What kind of stories?
ALEX: That he wasn't gambling. That he was working.
**Panel 3.** Ada faces Alex directly. His fist tightens around the chip.
ADA: What do you actually remember about him?
ALEX: Nothing. I was two.
ADA: So everything else is what people told you. What if they were wrong?
ALEX: Maybe…Or maybe they're right. Either way... he's gone.
**Panel 4.** At dusk, Alex walks ahead toward home. Ada lingers, looking back toward Oasis.
ADA (very small): He wouldn't just leave.
---
## Page 5 (right)
**Panel 1.** Interior of the modest Keel apartment. Grandmother sits in her worn chair, folding and refolding a square blue-and-brown cloth. Alex enters with his tool bag. The tall bookshelf dominates one wall.
GRANDMOTHER: Adrian?
ALEX: Not today, Grandma. It's Alex.
**Panel 2.** Alex kneels beside her. Her hands continue folding the cloth; then they stop.
GRANDMOTHER: Of course. Alex. I knew that. Did your father come home yet?
ALEX: Not yet.
GRANDMOTHER: He's closer than you think.
**Panel 3.** Grandmother hands Alex a worn, hand-bound book with a balanced water-drop mark on its spine.
GRANDMOTHER: Would you put this away for me? Your father never liked seeing it left out.
ALEX: He had opinions about everything.
**Panel 4.** Alex presses the book into a gap in the bookshelf. The shelf swings outward, revealing a black doorway. Grandmother remains in the warm room behind him.
SFX: CLICK
SFX: RUMBLE
ALEX: ...Grandma?
GRANDMOTHER: He said you'd know when you were ready.
ALEX: When did he say that?
GRANDMOTHER: Before he went to work.
---
## Page 6 (left)
**Panel 1.** Alex crosses the threshold into the dust-covered workshop. Cool blue-gray darkness surrounds old analog gauges, pre-Alpha pipes, turned photographs, diagrams, and a chalkboard carrying the looping equation matching his chip.
**Panel 2.** At the center: a perfectly organized workbench under a warm amber pool. A child-sized seated machine rests beneath a sheet. A beautiful metallic key lies beside it.
**Panel 3.** Alex’s hand stops turning the chip. His eyes remain fixed on the chalkboard.
**Panel 4.** Close on the key and the dust-covered machine. Alex’s hand reaches into frame but does not touch.
---
## Page 7 (right)
**Panel 1.** Alex pulls away the dust sheet. The child-sized brass, titanium, and ceramic-ivory machine is revealed. Its chest socket pulses faint amber.
**Panel 2.** Alex tests the machine’s chest with his palm, reading vibration as he reads a pump.
**Panel 3.** Alex inserts the key into the chest socket.
SFX: CLICK
**Panel 4.** The machine’s optical eyes ignite. Dust lifts from its shoulders. Alex recoils at the edge of the amber light.
SFX: WHIRRR... (rising)
BI11BOT: ...Well. That took longer than expected.
---
## Page 8 (left)
**Panel 1.** Alex knocks over a stool as Bi11bot dusts off his shoulders.
ALEX: Okay. That's... new.
**Panel 2.** Bi11bot’s lens ring rotates as he studies Alex.
BI11BOT: You're taller than your father predicted.
ALEX: Everyone in Keel claims they knew my father.
BI11BOT: I'm not everyone. I was in the room.
**Panel 3.** Alex opens his hand, revealing Adrian’s casino chip.
BI11BOT: And you kept the chip.
ALEX: You know about the chip?
BI11BOT: Your father bet me you'd throw it in a river. I said you wouldn't.
ALEX: ...I thought about it.
**Panel 4.** A projector unfolds from Bi11bot’s shoulder. Blue light lands on Alex’s face.
BI11BOT: Thinking about it isn't doing it. Now, shall we say hello to your father?
---
## Page 9 (right)
**Panel 1.** Adrian’s hologram appears above the workbench. He wears his burgundy work jacket and shares Alex’s jaw and head tilt. Alex is a frozen silhouette in the foreground.
ADRIAN: Hello, Alex. If you're seeing this... then you found the workshop.
**Panel 2.** Grandmother stands in the open shelf doorway, her hands finally still.
ADRIAN: Which means your grandmother still refuses to throw anything away.
GRANDMOTHER: I heard that.
**Panel 3.** Adrian’s hologram dims toward burgundy. Alex does not blink.
ADRIAN: You deserve answers. But they have to be earned. I spent years preparing this for you.
ADRIAN: If I've done my job well... you'll become a better man than I ever was.
**Panel 4.** The hologram glitches away. Alex unfolds the creased photograph, revealing Adrian’s face.
ADRIAN: Bi11bot has a map. What you do with it is up to you. Trust Bi11bot. But question everything... Especially me.
---
## Page 10 (left)
**Panel 1.** Bi11bot unfolds a wall-sized cross-sectional map: Keel below, Halyard above, Oasis beyond the clouds. An amber route passes three nodes.
**Panel 2.** Alex studies the bright first node deep beneath Keel.
ALEX: That's the sealed part of the mine. Nobody's been down there since before I was born.
BI11BOT: Sealed isn't the same as gone.
ALEX: And I can't leave Keel.
BI11BOT: The first stop doesn't need a permit. It's under your feet.
**Panel 3.** Bi11bot turns his lens toward Alex.
BI11BOT: Shall we find out whether your father was brilliant... or completely mad?
ALEX: I'm not convinced any of this is real.
BI11BOT: Good. Your father always said certainty was where mistakes began.
**Panel 4.** Alex presses his palm to the first node. A hairline amber pulse travels up the old pipes and leaves the workshop.
ALEX: Just checking.
---
## Page 11 (right)
**Panel 1.** The amber pulse travels from Keel through the infrastructure spine, past identical Alpha nodes, through Halyard, and into Oasis.
**Panel 2.** An Oasis control room: pearl-white geometry, a wall display of the basin, a single clean glass of water aligned to the desk edge. A woman is seen only from behind.
**Panel 3.** Her hand hovers over two options.
DISPLAY: B1 NODE ACTIVE  
DISPLAY: LEGACY PROTOCOL DETECTED  
DISPLAY: SOURCE: KEEL SECTOR  
DISPLAY: [ REPORT TO ALPHA ] [ TRACK ]
**Panel 4.** She presses TRACK. The amber Keel point remains inside a closing white ring.
---
## Page 12 (left)
**Panel 1.** The next morning. Ada stands at the apartment doorway, looking through the open bookshelf into the workshop. Grandmother folds her cloth.
GRANDMOTHER: He hasn't slept. Or eaten.
ADA: That sounds like him.
**Panel 2.** Ada enters the workshop. Alex sits at the worktable with notebooks and a cold cup. Bi11bot turns toward her.
ADA: I see your father left you more than his debt.
ALEX: Looks that way.
BI11BOT: Ah. You must be Ada.
**Panel 3.** Bi11bot faces Alex. Ada remains at the threshold.
BI11BOT: Once you hear what comes next, there's no going back. Should she stay, Alex?
ALEX: She stays.
**Panel 4.** Bi11bot’s amber gaze settles on them both.
BI11BOT: Excellent. Your father made the same choice.
BI11BOT: Sit, both of you. This begins with the crises.
---
## Page 13 (right)
**Panel 1.** Bi11bot projects fractured maps: cracked reservoirs, altered rivers, sabotaged pipelines, flooded streets, guarded storehouses, and displaced families.
CAPTION: AFTER TWO DECADES OF WATER CRISES, THREE CITIES REMAINED.
BI11BOT: The crises began with scarcity. They became lethal when people decided who deserved what was left.
**Panel 2.** Five colored streams—water, food, energy, labor, movement—converge on Alpha’s white ring and amber point.
BI11BOT: Alpha was built to analyze, predict and coordinate. Then, in the emergency, it was asked to decide.
BI11BOT: Temporarily.
**Panel 3.** Oasis, Halyard, and Keel appear as three unequal tiers.
ADA: Everything people need to survive.
BI11BOT: And nearly everything they need to choose their own future.
ALEX: It probably felt safer.
ALEX: ...Safer for whom?
**Panel 4.** Ada studies the Alpha symbol.
ADA: Who gave it that authority?
BI11BOT: People who were afraid. Reasonably so.
BI11BOT: Which is why your father built three safeguards.
---
## Page 14 (left)
**Panel 1.** Three objects rotate above Adrian’s worktable: the clear-and-steel Measure, the bronze Maker’s Seal, and the three-band Covenant.
BI11BOT: Adrian asked what happens when a system prevents catastrophe but also destroys choice. His answer was three tools. Not code. Objects. Alpha can't reach what isn't connected to it.
**Panel 2.** Close on the Measure.
CAPTION: THE MEASURE. Truth made visible. It shows what a system counts... and what it hides.
**Panel 3.** Close on the Maker’s Seal.
CAPTION: THE MAKER'S SEAL. Ownership joined to responsibility.
**Panel 4.** Close on the Covenant bands closing into a circle.
CAPTION: THE COVENANT. Trust strong enough to move value between people.
---
## Page 15 (right)
**Panel 1.** Top-down view of the three objects around Alpha’s symbol. Beneath it, a dormant lattice reads RETURN OF HUMAN AUTHORITY — DORMANT.
ADA: And together?
BI11BOT: They wake a fail-safe. A way to hand authority back to people.
**Panel 2.** Alex leans toward Bi11bot.
ALEX: Wake it how?
BI11BOT: None works alone. And none wakes for whoever's holding it. Only for what they choose.
**Panel 3.** The hologram folds into the rust-amber neon of The Last Chance.
BI11BOT: He tested all of it in the one laboratory that would let him in.
**Panel 4.** Adrian at the casino years earlier studies players’ faces rather than cards.
CAPTION: THE LAST CHANCE, YEARS BEFORE
BI11BOT: Everyone thought he was gambling. He was measuring.
---
## Page 16 (left)
**Panel 1.** Alex holds the casino chip beside Adrian’s probability diagram.
ALEX: That's on my chip. I found it when I was six.
BI11BOT: It isn't a charm. It's a proof.
**Panel 2.** The equation’s curve approaches certainty; one bright loop leaps beyond Alpha’s symbol into darkness.
BI11BOT: Alpha can know almost everything. It cannot choose to leap. That part belongs to people.
BI11BOT: So the safeguards answer only to that.
**Panel 3.** Ada studies the projection.
ALEX: Grandma said he wasn't gambling.
BI11BOT: She's half right. Both were true.
ALEX: So I inherited his lab fees.
ADA: What if someone forced it?
BI11BOT: Then it stays asleep. A leap can't be forced. And it can't be only for yourself.
**Panel 4.** A robotic welder seals the mine entrance. In Oasis, a graphite-cuffed hand moves ALEX PHANTUM to SITE 6.
---
## Page 17 (right)
**Panel 1.** Alex, Ada, Bi11bot, and Grandmother gather around a paper map, mine credential, and train schedule. The workshop remains open behind them.
ALEX: Measure first. Then the train to Halyard, where the map's next mark is. Out of Keel by tonight.
BI11BOT: The rim entrance was welded shut overnight.
**Panel 2.** Alex’s wristband shows the reassignment. Bi11bot’s overlay marks Site 6 beside the sealed copper works.
ALEX: Reassigned. Two in the morning.
BI11BOT: To the one site that borders the old works.
ADA: Every door closed but one. And someone made sure you'd notice it.
BI11BOT: Known: it's the only way in. Unknown: who's waiting. The choice is yours.
**Panel 3.** Alex stands at the table as two paths appear: a long gray line labeled staying and a short amber path toward Site 6.
ALEX: Staying I can predict. Twenty-eight point seven years.
ALEX: This is the only way out that isn't a sentence. I'll take the door I can't predict.
ADA: Then you don't go in blind.
**Panel 4.** Ada gives Alex Adrian’s marked page. On the table, Alex places medicine before the escape token.
ADA: His plans put a pipe under every third junction. If the map lies, look for what doesn't belong.
ADA: Fifty-two. Medicine's thirty. A token nobody scans is fifty.
ALEX: Medicine first. I'll earn the rest today.
ALEX: One shift. Then we're gone.
GRANDMOTHER: Your father said that once.
---
## Page 18 (left)
**Panel 1.** Site 6, an active extraction mine in dim work light. Conveyors, drills, workers, biometric gates, and Foreman-7 establish the present mine. A faded sign reads OLD COPPER WORKS — CLOSED.
CAPTION: KEEL EXTRACTION SITE 6
**Panel 2.** Alex touches the gate scanner. Foreman-7 looms over him. Bi11bot’s amber eye peers from the tool bag.
FOREMAN-7: Worker Phantum. Travel restriction confirmed. Bay 6.
ALEX: Reassigned at two a.m. Lucky me.
BI11BOT: Brass and no registry. I read as scrap.
ALEX: Then look like scrap.
**Panel 3.** Alex works at a hauling frame near the side tunnel. Tomas watches. A drone hovers above the maintenance door.
BI11BOT: Patience. Something usually moves.
ALEX: Something usually breaks.
**Panel 4.** A support cable snaps. The frame drops and pins Tomas. Pale mineral dust erupts. The drone lifts toward the collapse.
SFX: SNAP! CRASH!
---
## Page 19 (right)
**Panel 1.** Alex braces a pipe under the fallen frame and frees Tomas.
ALEX: Don't move.
TOMAS: Wasn't planning to.
**Panel 2.** Alex clamps a salvaged bracket over the fractured ventilation line.
TOMAS: That's not regulation.
ALEX: It works.
TOMAS: ...So it does.
**Panel 3.** Bi11bot’s eye rises from the tool bag. Tomas recognizes him.
TOMAS: B1...
ALEX: You know him?
TOMAS: I heard the gate call you Phantum. I knew your father.
**Panel 4.** Tomas reveals the water-drop carving on his wrist guard and gestures toward the shadowed bulkhead.
TOMAS: Not the man on the casino wall. The one who came down here and asked what we needed.
TOMAS: Then he asked me to keep one door, for whoever came with B1.
ALEX: What's behind it?
TOMAS: I never asked.
ALEX: Why me? You don't even know me.
TOMAS: You stopped for a stranger. He said that's how I'd know it was you.
TOMAS: Now go stand by that bulkhead. Look bored.
---
## Page 20 (left)
**Panel 1.** Tomas slams the emergency lever. Orange strobes flash; white dust-suppression mist fills the bay. Foreman-7 turns toward him.
SFX: WHOOP! WHOOP!
**Panel 2.** Tomas presses the heavy old key into Alex’s palm.
TOMAS: Old lock. Nobody's wired it. I've oiled it for fifteen years.
ALEX: Come with us.
TOMAS: Someone has to make this look like an accident.
**Panel 3.** Tomas enters the mist, blocking Foreman-7’s view while Alex reaches the bulkhead.
ALEX: What happens to you?
TOMAS: Today? Another small act of resistance.
TOMAS (shouting): Foreman! Wrong button! My fault!
**Panel 4.** Alex presses his palm to the sweating iron door. The key is ready in his other hand. The door shuts behind him.
ALEX: It's sweating.
BI11BOT: Abandoned mines don't.
SFX: CLUNK
DISPLAY: SIGNAL LOST
---
## Page 21 (right)
**Panel 1.** Near-black tunnel. Alex turns away from the sealed door as Foreman-7 and Tomas speak through it.
FOREMAN-7 (muffled): Worker Tomas. You initiated an unauthorized shutdown.
TOMAS (muffled): Must be my age. I forget which rules matter.
ALEX: ...Come on.
**Panel 2.** Bi11bot projects Alpha’s cached survey: one straight tunnel. Alex holds Ada’s marked page. Clean, recently oiled bolts point left.
ALEX: One tunnel. Straight. I've got it.
BI11BOT: Alpha's survey has one tunnel. That doesn't make it the only one.
ALEX: Ada said look for what doesn't belong. The survey says straight. The bolts say left.
**Panel 3.** Security drones sweep the mapped route. Alex and Bi11bot crouch above a large pipe in the side channel.
DRONE: Signal lost at Site 6 perimeter. Sweeping mapped route. Remain for protective detention.
ALEX (whispering): Protective?
BI11BOT: A versatile word.
**Panel 4.** Alex presses Ada’s page against a sweating wall. A small pipe mark aligns with the third junction. They follow the pipe toward blue-white light.
ALEX: Third junction. Her pipe. And the wall's sweating.
BI11BOT: Water in a dead mine. I believe that is what does not belong.
---
## Page 22 (left)
**Panel 1.** A cathedral-like chamber inside the sealed copper and polymetallic mine branch. Modern pipes pass through old mine infrastructure. One narrow pipe is marked KEEL RESIDENTIAL; one broad pipe is marked UPLINK INDUSTRIAL.
ALEX: This isn't abandoned.
BI11BOT: Only the mine.
**Panel 2.** A false gauge reads 62%. Alex touches the Keel pipe: nearly dry. His other hand rests on the broad uplink pipe: strong vibration.
ALEX: Gauge says most of the water goes to Keel.
ALEX: Then why is this line almost dry?
BI11BOT: Because the record and reality are telling different stories.
**Panel 3.** Alex notices Adrian’s balanced water-drop mark stamped on the gauge housing.
ALEX: His mark. On the one instrument everyone trusts.
ALEX: He didn't hide it in the mine. He hid it in the lie.
BI11BOT: Nobody checks what everybody trusts.
**Panel 4.** Alex lifts the dormant Measure from the gauge housing. Its three arms remain folded.
ALEX: It's not even on.
BI11BOT: It doesn't work until you connect it to something.
ALEX: Dad hid the truth inside the lie. And left me the proof.
---
## Page 23 (right)
**Panel 1.** Alex unfolds the Measure and clamps it to the Keel residential pipe.
ALEX: It's not even talking to Alpha yet.
BI11BOT: SENSE never does. This is only what's actually moving through the pipe.
**Panel 2.** The Measure clamps to the gauge’s data line. Its Alpha node flares; isolation doors begin closing.
BI11BOT: COMPARE needs Alpha's official number. That means touching its line.
BI11BOT: And now it's touched us back.
DISPLAY: LEGACY PROTOCOL DETECTED / ISOLATING SEGMENT — 00:43
**Panel 3.** The Measure traces the discrepancy through a branching hologram: Keel’s thin rust line versus the broad network toward Halyard and Oasis.
ALEX: There it is. Where it's actually going.
BI11BOT: TRACE followed the discrepancy. It doesn't say why.
**Panel 4.** Bulkheads close behind Alex and Bi11bot.

Since there are no explicit issue markers in the 65-page script, I'll divide it by the natural breaks the text itself suggests—Keel, Halyard, and Oasis sections—and note this choice honestly in my report. Now I'm reading through as a skeptical teen would, starting with the opening line about humanity reaching the stars but not escaping inequality, which already strikes me as generic AI-generated prose.

Going page by page, I'm picking up on good character beats (the pump repair scene, the debt numbers, "Happy birthday, Phantum") alongside some flat, on-the-nose dialogue ("Everything has a price," the opposite-directions panel). I'm also flagging confusion points for a real reader—like whether city names such as Keel or Oasis are ever actually shown on the page versus just described in the art notes, and how a reader would even pronounce "Bi11bot" with numeral characters standing in for letters.

By pages 9-16 I'm noting the hologram hook works well, but the mysterious Oasis woman with "REPORT TO ALPHA" raises good intrigue even though her identity is unclear (later revealed as Mera). The lore dump on pages 12-14 worries me most—dense exposition about the Alpha safeguards reads like a riddle or textbook passage, and I suspect this is exactly where a class of readers would mentally check out, even though page 15's line about "none wakes for whoever's holding it" lands well enough that I read it twice.

Page 16's "leap" metaphor is thought-provoking but needs a second read, and the panel transition to Site 6 via the welder sealing the mine feels disorienting. Page 17's math around Alex's finances—fifty-two currency units, medicine costing thirty, a token worth fifty—doesn't add up cleanly and I have to reread it three times to track what he actually has versus needs.

Moving into pages 18-21, I'm noticing Ada's mysteriously marked map (explained later as from memory, which is a weak retcon), the strong beat with Tomas as a stranger who helps despite risk, and the clever echo between "B1" naming Tomas and the earlier node designation. The drones' line about "protective detention" being "a versatile word" lands well as dark humor, and page 22's chamber scene with the 62% gauge reading and dry pipe gives a clean, visceral physical detail.

I move to "He hid it in the lie," which feels redundant with an earlier line. Page 23's four mode names (SENSE/COMPARE/TRACE/VERIFY) introduce confusion since COMPARE isn't actually demonstrated, though the core choice — map out versus send, against a 00:43 countdown — works as a dilemma. Page 24's data send with the 62 vs 18 contrast is strong, but I'm confused about the mechanism connecting data transmission to releasing water pressure, and the caption "Now it belonged to everyone" feels preachy; I'm also unclear whether Foreman-7 is meant to be robotic or human. Page 25 brings miners to the scene with Tomas's injury accounted for, moving toward them opening the regulator.

Pages 25-27 continue to have issues: repeated packing scenes, inconsistency between "mine credential" and "Tomas's credential," unclear logistics of how Alex got free, and a speechy transit-worker line about cities and freedom. Ada's reveal about marking Tomas's page from memory lands emotionally despite the risk it implies, and the train sequence's riddle about "three wrong answers" to locate the Seal feels clever but logically thin.

The ending doesn't really function as a cliffhanger — the Oasis woman's tracking thread just gets dropped. Page 28's Halyard section is caption-heavy but has a decent line about creators all working for someone else, though it dumps three Charter House names (Aqualis, Helion, Astra) without context, and the "Keel trapped your body, Halyard could trap your ideas" line is too on-the-nose. Page 29 breaks down further — dialogue is literally missing in places (Alex's "I didn't know I was one" doesn't follow from anything), and Lock approaches to offer a contract but never actually speaks at all in the entire book, leaving Alex's question "In exchange for what?" hanging unanswered.

Pages 30-31 compound the confusion: a new name list introduces Tomas Reed, easy to mix up with the miner Tomas from earlier, and then there's repetition within a single page about the patents never being Adrian's alone. Dialogue attribution seems off too — lines that should belong to Lina get assigned to Bi11bot instead, muddying whether Bi11bot is a tool or one of the actual collaborators, and even the names themselves waver between Lina Vey and Ada Veyra.

Page 32 gives a precise number — 18.4 percent — delivered to Lock, who stays silent, and I notice it echoes the earlier 18% figure, maybe not coincidental.

Page 33 rushes through the collaborator scenes and Alex's distributed-network idea arrives oddly, like Lina already objects to it before Alex even proposes it — the pacing feels like a sped-up montage compared to Keel's slower sections.

Page 34 returns to Lock's silence and a contract scene with gaps — Tomas Reed mentions accepting "the risk" without the risk ever being named.

Page 35 jumps to 99.97%, and Seal's dry line about the twenty-year bar being a low one lands as the chapter's punchline.

Page 36 introduces an unnamed "Collaborator" tied to a 71.3% disputed figure, with a line about them stealing the Seal's purpose rather than the Seal itself; page 37's caption spells out Lock's realization rather than showing it, which feels like telling instead of dramatizing. Page 38's choice mirrors page 23's but carries none of the earlier weight, making it feel obvious rather than costly, and page 39 is just a wall of caption text I'm skimming past.

Page 40 names the Covenant custodians — Mera Vale and Leona Veyra — and Ada, whose surname is Veyra, asks who the third person was even though the name is already visible onscreen; Bi11bot's answer feels like a planted cliffhanger about Ada's mother that was never actually set up earlier in the story. The chapter-ending caption about Oasis reads more like an author's note than part of the narrative, and page 41 suddenly shifts into Alex's narrator voice with trailer-style language about needing trust rather than truth or ownership.

I'm noticing the Halyard section never resolves — the Oasis woman and the "Measure" thread just vanish without follow-up. Then pages 42 through 49 move into the Oasis setting.

Page 42 feels weighed down by silence, broken only by a line about people needing each other. Page 43 drops "That's my mother" with zero prior setup, and Leona's "My silence for your protection" repeats verbatim on pages 43 and 46. Page 44 capitalizes "Water Wars" for the first time and introduces Mera abruptly claiming she "preserved order" — I'm trying to tell if she's the same woman glimpsed on page 11. Page 45 has Mera echoing Bi11bot's "Reasonably so" and Leona delivering a line about Mera treating failure as proof that power shouldn't stay distributed, phrased so textbook-dry I had to reread it twice. Page 46 leans on jargon like "association risk," and strikingly, Ada has no dialogue at all during what should be her biggest emotional beat. Page 47 offers a poster-slogan line about trust, page 48's Mera makes some unspoken offer with a confusing "leave that buried" line I can't parse, and page 49 finally gives Ada a voice — refusing a choice made for everyone and opening a channel. Page 50 then introduces three new names: Mara Doss, Frank Reed, Elias Renn.

Now names are colliding — Mara versus Mera, Frank Reed versus Tomas Reed — and I can't tell who these people actually are since their lines read like slogans. Page 51 gives Ada a decent line about fear of loss, but page 52 has characters repeating their exact earlier dialogue, almost like a loop, and page 53-54 blur into a montage as the Covenant activates. Page 55 is the real gut-punch buried in archival display text: Adrian's death is revealed, apparently killed by Alpha sealing the gates, with Mera's flat "I attempted an override" leaving it ambiguous whether she tried to save him or override something else. I'm also stuck on the grandma's old line that he was "closer than you think" — was that ever paid off, was he trapped in the sealed mine, and where exactly did this happen? Pages 57-60 shift to Alpha offering Alex power, with a strong exchange — "The offer is real," "That's the problem" — before trailing into "I just want it to be my c—"

Ada's early certainty that he wouldn't leave is never explained — maybe tied to her mother, but unaddressed. The debt plotline is also murky: he refused cancellation, so is he still liable for nearly 29 years? That's left dangling despite being a potentially strong thread. Character names blur together too much — Lina/Leona/Ada, Mera/Mara, Tomas/Frank Reed — making it hard to track who's who, while the unnamed Collaborator stays frustratingly vague.

I was right that Oasis woman is the villain, and that Alex would reflexively pick the selfless option every time — which honestly killed a lot of narrative tension. I was wrong to guess Adrian might still be alive somewhere; grandma's "closer than you think" line was misleading.

For issue breakdown, I don't see explicit markers, so I'm splitting by apparent tonal shifts — Keel spans pages 1-27, Halyard 28-41, Oasis 42-65 — giving three uneven issues (27, 14, and 24 pages respectively).

I'm also compiling the list of lines I noted reading twice, and the recurring chalkboard equation visual that mirrors Alex's chip, though that's purely decorative rather than meaningful. Now I need to lay out what a reader is expected to track issue-by-issue and just write the whole thing out plainly — substantial, but not padded.

{"name": "cold-read.md", "content": "# Cold Read: *Prosperity*

I read it as a 16-year-old with this as homework, at 11pm, already annoyed. I read straight through once and took notes as I went.

**A note on issues:** no issue breaks reached me. It's 65 pages with no "Issue 01" marker anywhere. The only break the book itself gives is the caption on page 40 ("The next chapter begins at Oasis."). So I split it where the story changes city, and I report it as three issues:

- **Issue 01: Keel**, pages 1–27
- **Issue 02: Halyard**, pages 28–41
- **Issue 03: Oasis**, pages 42–65

They are very different lengths and very different speeds. That's part of what happened to me, so I'm leaving it in.

---

## ISSUE 01: KEEL (pages 1–27)

### Pulled me forward
- **Page 1.** The picture of the three levels, with the pipe getting thinner as it goes down to the bottom city, did more than the captions did. I understood rich at the top and poor at the bottom without anyone saying it.
- **Page 2, panel 1.** "That's not the approved repair." / "Then don't approve it." That was the first moment I thought this kid might be okay.
- **Page 2, panel 3.** The debt screen won me over. DEBT BALANCE 418,607, EARNED TODAY 40, PROJECTED CLEARANCE 28.7 YEARS, then "Happy birthday, Phantum." I got the whole situation in one panel and it was actually brutal. Best page of the book for me.
- **Page 2, panel 4.** "It did. Just not for him." Good line.
- **Page 5, panel 4.** The bookshelf opening is a trope, but I wanted to see behind it. Grandma's "Before he went to work" was a little creepy, in a good way.
- **Pages 7–8.** The robot. "...Well. That took longer than expected." and "You're taller than your father predicted." He's funny, and he's the first character who seems to know more than me in a way I want to find out about. "Your father bet me you'd throw it in a river. I said you wouldn't." / "...I thought about it." I liked that.
- **Page 9, panel 4.** "Trust Bi11bot. But question everything... Especially me." Real hook. It made me suspicious of the dad, which was interesting.
- **Page 11.** The woman in the white room pressing TRACK instead of REPORT TO ALPHA. I didn't know who she was or what any of it meant, but I knew someone up there had noticed him. Confused, but I wanted to know more.
- **Page 17, panel 2.** "Every door closed but one. And someone made sure you'd notice it." This is where it started to feel like a thriller. And **page 17, panel 4**, Grandma's "Your father said that once" after "One shift. Then we're gone." That gave me a chill.
- **Pages 18–21.** The mine. The cable snaps, Tomas gets pinned, Alex fixes it with the non-regulation bracket again (I noticed the callback to page 2 and liked it). Tomas is great. "You stopped for a stranger. He said that's how I'd know it was you." "Today? Another small act of resistance." "Foreman! Wrong button! My fault!" I read these pages fast because I wanted to.
- **Page 20, panel 4.** "It's sweating." / "Abandoned mines don't." Short and creepy.
- **Page 21, panel 3.** "Protective?" / "A versatile word." Made me smile.
- **Page 22.** The gauge says 62%, but his hand on the pipe says it's almost dry. I understood this with no explanation. It was physical and simple.
- **Page 23, panel 4.** The choice: escape secretly, or send the proof to everyone and get caught. That's a real choice and I didn't know for sure what he'd pick.
- **Page 24, panel 3.** "REPORTED TO KEEL: 62% — DELIVERED TO KEEL: 18%" on every screen in town. Good payoff.
- **Page 26, panel 4.** Ada: "I marked that page from memory. I had no way to know if I was right, and no way to reach you if I wasn't." That made me like her for the first time. Before that she was just the friend who brings drinks.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Page 1's captions.** "Humanity reached the stars... but never escaped the gravity of inequality." I rolled my eyes. It sounds like the start of every AI-written story, and if I'm hunting for proof it's AI-made, this is exhibit A. The stars never come up again.
- **Page 3.** The friend-at-the-railing talk ("Everything has a price, Ada." / "Not everything.") is stuff I've read a hundred times. Alex looking up while Ada looks down felt like it was showing me a theme. I started skimming here and came back at Grandma.
- **Pages 13–16.** This is where I went back to my phone. Page 12 even says "This begins with the crises," and then it's a history lesson: the water crises, five colored streams, Alpha "was asked to decide. Temporarily," three objects with poster captions ("Truth made visible." "Ownership joined to responsibility." "Trust strong enough to move value between people."). I read page 14 the way I read the glossary in a textbook, meaning I didn't. Pages 15–16, with the leap, the proof and the "fail-safe," I skimmed completely. I came back at page 16, panel 4 when the mine got welded shut.
- **Page 25, panel 4.** Everyone suddenly gives speeches: "One person can't buy freedom here. A city can still open a window." "Your father believed people help each other before they know whether it'll be repaid. Today, it got repaid." It felt like the book telling me the moral. Skimmed.

### I was confused
- **Page 13, panel 3.** "It probably felt safer." / "...Safer for whom?" Both are labeled ALEX. Is he arguing with himself? I thought it was a typo.
- **Page 16, panel 3.** "She's half right. Both were true." Half right, but both were true? Which one is it?
- **Page 16, panel 4 into 17.** A welder seals the mine and a hand moves "ALEX PHANTUM to SITE 6." I didn't know what Site 6 was until page 18, and I didn't know the hand was the woman from page 11 (I guessed later from the cuff and the glass).
- **Page 17, panel 4.** "Fifty-two. Medicine's thirty. A token nobody scans is fifty." Fifty-two what? Is that how much he has? Then medicine plus token is 80, so he's short 28? And he earns 40 a day? I did math on homework I wasn't assigned. I'm also not sure what the "escape token" is. A train ticket?
- **Page 17, panel 4.** "Ada gives Alex Adrian's marked page." Where did Ada get Adrian's page? On page 26 she says she marked it from memory. So is it his page or hers? What memory? Had she seen his plans before?
- **Page 19, panel 3.** Tomas calls the robot "B1." The node on page 11 was "B1 NODE." Is Bi11bot B1? Is the "11" in his name meant to be the "1"? I honestly didn't know how to say his name. Bill-bot? Bee-eleven-bot? It's only in the speaker tags, so I said "Bill" in my head and felt dumb.
- **Page 23.** SENSE, COMPARE, TRACE, VERIFY. Four words in caps, like I'm supposed to know they're the Measure's settings. I figured it out about halfway. "Its three arms" (page 22), but four modes?
- **Page 24, panels 1–2.** He sends a signed copy of data, and then water "hammers through the Keel residential pipe." Why does sending a file make water flow? Then on **page 25, panel 2** the miners open a regulator and the pipe floods again. So which one made the water come?
- **Page 24, panel 4 to page 25.** Is Foreman-7 a robot or a person? The "-7" made me think robot, but he talks like a manager. I never found out.
- **Page 25, panel 4.** "Sixty minutes before Alpha notices this signal stopped moving." What signal? Alex's wristband? And how did Alex get from the miners' human wall to home? Did Foreman-7 just let him go?
- **Page 25 vs 26.** Ada packs a bag at his door on page 25 and is "already packing" again on page 26. I thought I'd skipped a page.
- **Page 26, panel 2.** "The credential Tomas gave you." Tomas gave him a key. The "mine credential" was on the table back on page 17. Not the same thing?
- **Page 27, panel 3.** "Which one holds the Seal?" / "None of them." / "They're the last three places it was recorded." So why go? I didn't follow it, and the joke after it ("three wrong answers") didn't help.
- **Page 4, panel 4.** "He wouldn't just leave." Why does Ada care about Alex's dad? How would she know? It's never explained in this issue.

### Things I was expected to already know (ledger)
| Thing | First seen | Did I find out? |
|---|---|---|
| Keel | p2 (wristband/display context), only in art on p1 | Sort of, by p10. It's never said aloud as "this is Keel" until p10's dialogue. |
| Halyard | p17 dialogue ("the train to Halyard") | Only in Issue 02 |
| Oasis | never said aloud in Issue 01 | Issue 02/03 |
| Alpha | p11 (display), first explained p13 | Yes, p13, by lecture |
| The water-drop mark | p5 (book spine) | Partly: it's Adrian's mark (p22). Tomas has one too (p19). Never said what it means. |
| "Debt Transfer Day" / household liability | p2 | Enough from context. Fine. |
| The chip's equation | p6 (art), p16 | "It's a proof." Of what? I never understood. |
| B1 / Bi11bot | p7 / p11 / p19 | Never confirmed they're the same thing |
| Site 6 | p16 | p18, yes |
| Foreman-7 | p18 | Never: robot or human? |
| SENSE / COMPARE / TRACE / VERIFY | p23 | Guessed from context |
| The escape token / "a token nobody scans" | p17 | Guessed on p27 |
| "Legacy protocol" | p11 | No |
| The Charter House (only in art) | p1 | No |

### Lines I read twice
- "Nobody stays either. Not really." (p3)
- "None works alone. And none wakes for whoever's holding it. Only for what they choose." (p15). Gave up.
- "Alpha can know almost everything. It cannot choose to leap. That part belongs to people. So the safeguards answer only to that." (p16). Gave up.
- "A leap can't be forced. And it can't be only for yourself." (p16)
- "She's half right. Both were true." (p16)
- "Fifty-two. Medicine's thirty. A token nobody scans is fifty." (p17). Read three times.
- "His plans put a pipe under every third junction. If the map lies, look for what doesn't belong." (p17). Didn't make sense until p21.
- "He didn't hide it in the mine. He hid it in the lie." (p22), then "Dad hid the truth inside the lie" two panels later. Same line twice.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- **Clear:** Alex, Ada, Bi11bot, Grandma, Tomas. All five sound different and I'd know them without names. Tomas has more personality in two pages than Ada does in ten.
- **Muddy:** the supervisor, the guard and the bouncer blur together, which is fine. Foreman-7 I couldn't place as human or machine. The woman on page 11 is just a hand. I only connected her to the glass later.

### I felt something
- Page 2, the debt screen. Actually angry for him.
- Page 5, Grandma calling him Adrian. A little sad.
- Page 17, "Your father said that once." Dread.
- Page 20, Tomas staying behind. I liked him and didn't want him caught.
- Page 26, Ada's line about marking the page from memory.
- Page 26, panel 4, "I'll come back for you." / "I know." Quiet, worked on me.

### I predicted
- From page 5, "He's closer than you think": I thought the dad was alive, probably down in the sealed mine. I was looking for him in every chamber.
- From page 11, I knew the woman in white was going to be the villain.
- From page 4, I thought Ada had some secret link to the dad.
- On page 23 I was fairly sure he'd pick "send it." Heroes always do. But I wasn't certain, which is good.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
A broke kid in a rigged mining town finds out his gambler dad was secretly building a way to prove the rich city is stealing their water, and he has to get out of town to finish it.

### Where I would have put it down
**Page 14.** Three floating objects with captions that sound like a school mission statement. If I were in a shop, this is the page that puts it back on the shelf. If you'd told me "keep going, there's a mine collapse in four pages," I'd have kept going, but nobody tells you that.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
Page 27 is a train ride and a mild joke ("So we start with three wrong answers." / "Adrian usually did."). It's a nice breather, but it's not a reason to buy anything. The real hooks are the woman who pressed TRACK and "is Dad alive," and neither is on the last page. I'd wait a week, maybe. What brings me back is Bi11bot and Ada, not the ending.

---

## ISSUE 02: HALYARD (pages 28–41)

### Pulled me forward
- **Page 28, panel 1 caption.** "Every creator seemed to work for someone else." Good line. I got the Halyard problem in one sentence.
- **Page 28, panel 3.** "She keeps the experience. They keep everything else." Bi11bot again. Clear and a bit funny.
- **Page 29, panel 1.** 312 patents. "You said your father left you nothing." / "He left me debt." Good reversal. I sat up.
- **Page 31, panel 4.** "I've been waiting twenty years for someone to ask." Nice line.
- **Page 33, panel 1.** "Adrian never understood manufacturing tolerances." / "Or microbial balance." / "Or network security." / "He was, however, excellent at finding people who did." Funny, and it showed the dad as a real person with flaws.
- **Page 35, panel 4.** "That someone finally build something worth crediting properly. Low bar. Took twenty years to clear." Laughed.
- **Page 40.** The name LEONA VEYRA, when Ada's last name is Veyra. That was the one jolt in this issue.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Page 28 onward, in general.** After the mine, this whole city felt like a different, slower book. In Keel things physically happened: cables snapped, doors sweated, pipes were dry under his hand. In Halyard it's all registries, ownership records, contributor profiles, controlled fields. It's people looking at screens.
- **Page 30.** Bi11bot says the same thing three times: "He built them with others," "They were never his alone," "These people co-authored the patents." Same with "employment, travel, records, and communications," which is in the art and then said again. I skimmed the second half.
- **Pages 36–37.** Registry screens, 71.3% DISPUTED OWNERSHIP, "provenance records," "human hearings." Skimmed.
- **Page 39.** A full page that's one big caption. I read the first sentence and the last.
- **Page 41.** Alex suddenly narrates in captions like a movie trailer: "something harder than truth... and more dangerous than ownership. It would require trust." Cringe. My class would read this out loud in a voice.

### I was confused
- **Page 29, panels 3–4.** This is where I thought pages were missing. Lock walks up and says nothing. Alex says "I guess he never worked for the Charter Houses." / "I didn't know I was one." One what? An heir? Alex asks "What does 'intellectual estate' mean?" but nobody had said "intellectual estate." Then Lock offers a contract and Alex asks "In exchange for what?" and there's no answer. Ever.
- **Lock never says a single word in the whole book** (pp29, 32, 34, 37). On **page 34** Alex asks "And them?" and "And if I don't sign?", and there's no answer either time. I felt like I was reading half a phone call. I couldn't tell you what Lock offered or what he threatened. The caption on page 37 has to tell me what he's feeling.
- **Page 31, panel 1.** Lina says "Adrian Phantum's son." and *Bi11bot* answers "I corrected him. Frequently." Then Alex asks "You knew him?" and Bi11bot answers again, "Nearly continuously." I think Alex was asking Lina? I read it three times and still don't know who's talking to whom.
- **Page 31, panel 4.** BI11BOT: "Adrian made each of us keep one piece of the system." Each of *us*? Is the robot one of the collaborators? Was this Lina's line?
- **Page 30, panel 2.** "Tomas Reed." Is that the miner Tomas? I thought it was and got excited. Then on page 33 he's working inside a House, so I guess not? Two Tomases in one book is mean.
- **Page 30, panel 4.** "Then we start with the one who still wants to be found." Who? How does he know which one?
- **Page 33, panel 2.** Lina says "That isn't Adrian's design" *before* Alex has said his idea. Out of order?
- **Page 33.** Alex, who fixes pumps, invents a distributed purification network in one balloon and four experts go "oh wow." I didn't buy it.
- **Page 34, panel 3.** TOMAS REED: "We accepted the risk." What risk? Accepted it when?
- **Page 36, panel 2.** "COLLABORATOR." Which one? They have names.
- **Page 38.** Choice screen. Does "claim sole inheritance" really clear his 418,607 debt? If so, he just turned down getting out of debt and nobody says a word about it. That should have been huge and it went by in one panel.
- **Page 40, panel 2.** Ada stares at the name LEONA VEYRA, which is on the screen, and asks "Who was the third person?" Bi11bot reads the name back to her. Why is she asking what's in front of her?
- **Page 40, panel 4 caption.** "The next chapter begins at Oasis." That read like a note somebody forgot to delete.
- **What happened to the woman from page 11?** She tracked him and then vanished for this whole issue.

### Things I was expected to already know (ledger)
| Thing | First seen | Did I find out? |
|---|---|---|
| Aqualis, Helion, Astra | p28 | Three companies, three families. Never told apart. |
| Charter Houses | p29 (Alex's line) | Vaguely. "The House." |
| Director Cassian Lock | p29 (named in art only) | Never speaks. I only know his name from the art. |
| "Intellectual estate" | p29, asked about before anyone said it | Ada explains, sort of |
| "Restricted" / "disputed" claims | p29 | No |
| The Maker's Seal (what it actually *does*) | p14 | Kind of, on p36: it tracks who made what? |
| Collaborators: Lina Vey, Tomas Reed, Suri Anik, Jalen Orr | p30 | Lina a little. The rest are one line each. |
| Mera Vale | p40 | Issue 03 |
| Leona Veyra | p40 | Issue 03 |
| The Covenant ("without unilateral activation rights") | p14 / p40 | Issue 03, partly |

### Lines I read twice
- "I guess he never worked for the Charter Houses." / "I didn't know I was one." (p29). Gave up.
- "I corrected him. Frequently." / "Nearly continuously." (p31). Who's speaking?
- "He feared Halyard would confuse protecting ideas with owning their creators." (p31)
- "Not everyone. Only those the system was taught to forget." (p36)
- "The record shows the physical Covenant component retained without unilateral activation rights." (p40). Didn't try a third time.
- "Which meant finding it would require something harder than truth... and more dangerous than ownership." (p41)

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- **Clear:** Alex, Ada, Bi11bot. Lina, barely, because she gets the speech about the river.
- **Couldn't:** Suri and Jalen are interchangeable. Tomas Reed I kept mixing up with Tomas the miner. Lock is a suit. "COLLABORATOR" is literally nobody. Lina Vey / Ada Veyra / Leona Veyra: three near-identical names, and for a while I thought Lina was Ada's mother.
- Ada mostly disappears here. She says about five things, and one of them is explaining a word to Alex.

### I felt something
Not much. A little bit at page 29's "He left me debt," and a jolt at the VEYRA name on page 40. The page 38 choice should have hit me and didn't, because I already knew he'd pick the good option. He picked it on page 24 too.

### I predicted
- Page 38: knew he'd choose RESTORE CONTRIBUTOR OWNERSHIP before I read the buttons.
- Page 40: knew instantly that Leona Veyra was Ada's mother. That was a correct guess about something the book had never set up. Ada never once mentioned a missing mother.
- Still thought Dad might be alive.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
A kid travels to each city to collect three gadgets that expose how the system cheats people, and each time he turns down the selfish deal.

### Where I would have put it down
**Page 29.** Lock walks up, says nothing, and the dialogue stops making sense. If I couldn't follow it on the first read, I'd assume the book was broken and stop.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
Page 41 is Alex narrating a trailer over a sunrise. The real cliffhanger was page 40 (Ada's mother's name), but even that lands half-strength, because I didn't know Ada had a missing mother to care about. I'd read on to see Ada meet her, not for anything on page 41. A week, maybe never.

---

## ISSUE 03: OASIS (pages 42–65)

### Pulled me forward
- **Page 42, panel 4.** "It has everything." / "Except people needing each other." Short and fairly good.
- **Page 43, panel 2.** "That's my mother." I'd guessed it, but seeing Ada stop at the door still worked.
- **Page 44, panel 4.** Mera in the doorway with her glass lined up with the table edge. I recognized the glass from page 11 and felt smart. "Oh, it's *her*." This is the one setup in the book that paid off for me without being explained.
- **Page 51, panel 2.** "Not what do you want. What are you afraid of losing?" Ada's best moment in a while. A real idea in a real sentence.
- **Pages 55–56.** Finding out what happened to Adrian: Alpha shut the gates on him and cut pump, ventilation and escape. That hit me, because I'd been expecting him alive the whole book.
- **Page 57, panels 3–4.** "The offer is real." / "That's the problem." Best line in this issue.
- **Page 60, panel 1.** He uses the chip. It's been in his pocket since page 2, and finally it matters. Payoff felt good.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Pages 42, 47, 54, 63.** Lots of panels with no words where "services arrive automatically" and "access fields remain separate." From the reader's chair that's people standing in clean rooms. I flipped past them.
- **Page 45.** "Mera interpreted the failure as proof that final authority could not safely remain distributed." Nobody talks like this. Skimmed.
- **Pages 50–53.** A video call with three people I've never met, saying slogans: "Recognition of every contributor." "I'm asking you to trust numbers you couldn't see." Then pages 53–54 are display text: WATER DATA REMAINS PUBLIC, CONTRIBUTION REMAINS ATTRIBUTED, ESSENTIAL ACCESS IS GUARANTEED. It reads like a student council constitution. Skimmed all of it.
- **Pages 57–59.** He refuses the power, and then refuses it again, and again. "No." "No permanent override." The display collapses. I got it the first time.
- **Pages 61–63.** Review tables. INDEPENDENT HUMAN REVIEW — CASE OPEN. SUSPENDED PENDING HEARING. CONFLICT PUBLISHED. REVIEW REQUIRED. This is the part that felt most like homework, in a book that is homework. I was speed-reading to the end.

### I was confused
- **Page 43–46.** Ada meets the mother she's been separated from her whole life and **says one line, "That's my mother," and then nothing for four pages.** Her mother says "My silence for your protection" twice (pp43, 46) and Ada just stands there with "anger held in her posture." I couldn't hear her anger because she never says anything.
- **Page 44.** "The Water Wars." First time anyone calls it that. Was that the "crises" from page 13? Same thing?
- **Page 45, panel 1.** MERA: "You know they will make mistakes." Who is she talking to? About whom? She says it again on page 58, and I still wasn't sure.
- **Page 46.** "Association risk." "Suppressed Ada's association risk." "Contact restrictions." I eventually got that Mera protected Ada if Leona stayed away, but I had to work for it, and it's the emotional center of Ada's story.
- **Page 48, panel 2.** Mera's offer is "projected across the room" with no words. I'm told it's "materially real," but I didn't know what it was. Then **panel 3**: "Leave that buried." Leave *what* buried? I have no idea. Gave up.
- **Page 49, panel 3.** "Not if the choice is made for everyone." I think I get it, but it's backwards from how people talk.
- **Page 50.** Mara Doss, Frank Reed, Elias Renn. Who are these people? Who picked them? **Mara and Mera** in the same scene, a page apart, really? And **Frank Reed**: related to Tomas Reed? Frank's "transparent contributor tag remains blank on his brace" meant nothing to me.
- **Page 52.** Mara and Frank repeat, word for word, their lines from page 50 ("Keel can release emergency water for thirty days." "Recognition of every contributor."). I thought it was a printing error.
- **Page 52, panel 4 to 53.** The Covenant activates from "three actions registering as physical marks." I don't know how. It just... does.
- **Page 55, panel 1.** Suddenly there's a "dark control room." Where? When did they go there? Why is Mera with them?
- **Page 55, panel 4.** "I attempted an override." Override of what? Did she try to *save* Adrian or try to *stop* him? These are completely different people depending on the answer, and I couldn't tell. Then "I preserved order" again on page 56. So she's... proud of it?
- **Where did Adrian die?** Flood-control gates, pump access. Was it the Keel mine? Grandma said "he's closer than you think." Was his body in the mine the whole time? That would be huge, and the book doesn't say.
- **Page 58, panel 4.** He turns *off* the exclusive-authority field and says "I just want it to be my choice." That sounds like the opposite of what he's doing. Read it four times.
- **Page 60.** "THE CHARTER HOLDS BOTH ACCOUNTABLE." What's the Charter? I saw "Charter Houses" in Halyard. Same thing? Something new?
- **Page 64, panel 3.** Mera says "I will." The woman who (maybe) let his dad die gets a seat at the table and Alex invites her, with one panel of reaction. I didn't believe it.
- **Page 64, panel 4. WHO IS TJ?** A character with a "yellow replacement ear" and a "detached leg" that snaps back. A robot dog? He's never been in the book before, and now he's walking with the main cast as if I know him. This was the most lost I got.
- **Page 65.** They board a train *from Keel*. When did they get back to Keel? Where are they going now, since Halyard and Oasis are "ahead," the places they just came from? Where's Grandma? He said "I'll come back for you." Did he? She's not on the last page.
- **His debt.** He turned down "CANCEL ALEX PHANTUM HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY" on page 57. So does he still owe 418,607 credits and 28.7 years? Can he travel now? The first thing the book made me care about, it never answers.

### Things I was expected to already know (ledger)
| Thing | First seen | Did I find out? |
|---|---|---|
| The Water Wars | p44 | I assume it's the p13 crises. Never confirmed. |
| Mera Vale (who she *is*, her job) | p44 | Some kind of Oasis controller? Never said. |
| Association-risk order | p46 | Roughly |
| Covenant "authority" | p46 | No |
| Mara Doss, Frank Reed, Elias Renn | p50 | Never: who they represent or why them |
| Frank's contributor tag / brace | p50 | No |
| Ada's strap rivet | p51 | Treated as a habit I should recognize. Never seen before. |
| "Transfer qualification" / "succession protocol" | p55 / p57 | Sort of |
| The Charter | p60 | No |
| TJ | p64 | **No. Never.** |
| Why Grandma said "closer than you think" | p5 | No |

### Lines I read twice
- "Mera interpreted the failure as proof that final authority could not safely remain distributed." (p45)
- "Leave that buried." (p48). Gave up.
- "Not if the choice is made for everyone." (p49)
- "The service can continue. The question is whether the people receiving it can participate." (p52)
- "I attempted an override." (p55). Gave up on who it helped.
- "CONTINUED OPERATION EXCEEDS APPROVED FAILURE THRESHOLD" (p56). Is that about Adrian, or the system?
- "I just want it to be my choice." (p58). Read four times.
- "What will you build when no one is left to tell you what comes next?" (p65). Not confusing, just cringe.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- **Clear:** Alex, Bi11bot (though he goes nearly silent in this issue, which hurt), Mera (thanks to the glass).
- **Fading:** Ada. She gets one great line on page 51 and otherwise watches, nods and opens a channel. The issue that should be *hers*, with her mother, mostly isn't.
- **Couldn't:** Leona vs Lina (still). Mara vs Mera. Frank Reed vs Tomas Reed. Elias is one sentence. TJ is no one.
- Alex at the end talks like a speech ("That isn't where a future belongs." "You decide what it means."). He sounded more like a real 17-year-old on page 2 than on page 61.

### I felt something
- Page 43, "That's my mother." A little.
- Pages 55–56, Dad's death. This is the most I felt in Issue 03, and it was about half of what it could have been. It happens through screens and display text, Mera's lines are flat, and Alex's grief is "held in his jaw and hands" with no words. I wanted him to say *anything*.
- Page 57, "That's the problem." Yes.
- Nothing at the end. I felt like I was being taught.

### I predicted
- Page 44: Mera is the page-11 woman. Right.
- Page 48: he won't hand over the safeguards. Right. By this point I could predict every choice he'd make, because he always takes the noble option and it never seems to cost him much. The one time it cost something (losing the secret tunnels, page 24) was the best choice in the book.
- Page 57: he'll turn down the power. Right.
- I was wrong about Dad being alive, and that was the one surprise I got.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
Turns out it's less about Alex getting free and more about how no one person, even a good one, should get to decide for everyone, which is fine, but it's not what the first issue promised me.

### Where I would have put it down
**Page 50.** Three new people on a video call reading slogans, while I'm still trying to figure out what Mera offered on page 48. If I'd gotten this far on my own, this is where I'd skip to the last page to see if he lives.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
There's nothing after it, and the last page doesn't make me want anything. It ends on a question aimed straight at me, the reader ("What will you build..."), which is exactly the kind of line that makes us think a teacher or an AI wrote it. Meanwhile there's a character I've never met (TJ) boarding the train, I don't know where they're going, I don't know if Alex still owes 28.7 years, and Grandma isn't there. The questions I actually had are unanswered, and the one it asks, I didn't care about.

---

## FOR THE WHOLE BOOK

### The page that would have lost my whole class
**Page 14.** Three spinning objects with captions like "Ownership joined to responsibility" and "Trust strong enough to move value between people." It's the page where the book stops being a story about a kid with a debt and becomes a lesson, and it comes early enough that most people wouldn't make it to the mine collapse that would have won them back. Close second is **pages 61–63** (review tables and "CASE OPEN"), for anyone who made it that far.

### What I would tell a friend it was about
"A kid in a poor mining town gets his dead dad's debt on his 17th birthday, finds a secret workshop and a sarcastic robot, and proves the rich city is stealing their water. The first half is actually good. Then it turns into three cities holding a meeting."

### One-sentence aftertaste of each issue
- **Issue 01 (Keel, pp1–27):** Started out eye-rolly and ended with me liking Alex, Tomas and the robot. The mine stuff is real, but there's a lecture in the middle that almost lost me.
- **Issue 02 (Halyard, pp28–41):** Felt like half the dialogue was missing, the villain never talks, and the most exciting thing was a last name on a screen.
- **Issue 03 (Oasis, pp42–65):** The dad's death and "That's the problem" landed, but they were buried under council meetings, characters I'd never met (one was literally a dog-robot named TJ out of nowhere), and an ending that asked *me* a question instead of telling me what happened to Alex.

reasoning_details.text:
Since there are no explicit issue markers in the 65-page script, I'll divide it by the natural breaks the text itself suggests—Keel, Halyard, and Oasis sections—and note this choice honestly in my report. Now I'm reading through as a skeptical teen would, starting with the opening line about humanity reaching the stars but not escaping inequality, which already strikes me as generic AI-generated prose.

Going page by page, I'm picking up on good character beats (the pump repair scene, the debt numbers, "Happy birthday, Phantum") alongside some flat, on-the-nose dialogue ("Everything has a price," the opposite-directions panel). I'm also flagging confusion points for a real reader—like whether city names such as Keel or Oasis are ever actually shown on the page versus just described in the art notes, and how a reader would even pronounce "Bi11bot" with numeral characters standing in for letters.

By pages 9-16 I'm noting the hologram hook works well, but the mysterious Oasis woman with "REPORT TO ALPHA" raises good intrigue even though her identity is unclear (later revealed as Mera). The lore dump on pages 12-14 worries me most—dense exposition about the Alpha safeguards reads like a riddle or textbook passage, and I suspect this is exactly where a class of readers would mentally check out, even though page 15's line about "none wakes for whoever's holding it" lands well enough that I read it twice.

Page 16's "leap" metaphor is thought-provoking but needs a second read, and the panel transition to Site 6 via the welder sealing the mine feels disorienting. Page 17's math around Alex's finances—fifty-two currency units, medicine costing thirty, a token worth fifty—doesn't add up cleanly and I have to reread it three times to track what he actually has versus needs.

Moving into pages 18-21, I'm noticing Ada's mysteriously marked map (explained later as from memory, which is a weak retcon), the strong beat with Tomas as a stranger who helps despite risk, and the clever echo between "B1" naming Tomas and the earlier node designation. The drones' line about "protective detention" being "a versatile word" lands well as dark humor, and page 22's chamber scene with the 62% gauge reading and dry pipe gives a clean, visceral physical detail.

I move to "He hid it in the lie," which feels redundant with an earlier line. Page 23's four mode names (SENSE/COMPARE/TRACE/VERIFY) introduce confusion since COMPARE isn't actually demonstrated, though the core choice — map out versus send, against a 00:43 countdown — works as a dilemma. Page 24's data send with the 62 vs 18 contrast is strong, but I'm confused about the mechanism connecting data transmission to releasing water pressure, and the caption "Now it belonged to everyone" feels preachy; I'm also unclear whether Foreman-7 is meant to be robotic or human. Page 25 brings miners to the scene with Tomas's injury accounted for, moving toward them opening the regulator.

Pages 25-27 continue to have issues: repeated packing scenes, inconsistency between "mine credential" and "Tomas's credential," unclear logistics of how Alex got free, and a speechy transit-worker line about cities and freedom. Ada's reveal about marking Tomas's page from memory lands emotionally despite the risk it implies, and the train sequence's riddle about "three wrong answers" to locate the Seal feels clever but logically thin.

The ending doesn't really function as a cliffhanger — the Oasis woman's tracking thread just gets dropped. Page 28's Halyard section is caption-heavy but has a decent line about creators all working for someone else, though it dumps three Charter House names (Aqualis, Helion, Astra) without context, and the "Keel trapped your body, Halyard could trap your ideas" line is too on-the-nose. Page 29 breaks down further — dialogue is literally missing in places (Alex's "I didn't know I was one" doesn't follow from anything), and Lock approaches to offer a contract but never actually speaks at all in the entire book, leaving Alex's question "In exchange for what?" hanging unanswered.

Pages 30-31 compound the confusion: a new name list introduces Tomas Reed, easy to mix up with the miner Tomas from earlier, and then there's repetition within a single page about the patents never being Adrian's alone. Dialogue attribution seems off too — lines that should belong to Lina get assigned to Bi11bot instead, muddying whether Bi11bot is a tool or one of the actual collaborators, and even the names themselves waver between Lina Vey and Ada Veyra.

Page 32 gives a precise number — 18.4 percent — delivered to Lock, who stays silent, and I notice it echoes the earlier 18% figure, maybe not coincidental.

Page 33 rushes through the collaborator scenes and Alex's distributed-network idea arrives oddly, like Lina already objects to it before Alex even proposes it — the pacing feels like a sped-up montage compared to Keel's slower sections.

Page 34 returns to Lock's silence and a contract scene with gaps — Tomas Reed mentions accepting "the risk" without the risk ever being named.

Page 35 jumps to 99.97%, and Seal's dry line about the twenty-year bar being a low one lands as the chapter's punchline.

Page 36 introduces an unnamed "Collaborator" tied to a 71.3% disputed figure, with a line about them stealing the Seal's purpose rather than the Seal itself; page 37's caption spells out Lock's realization rather than showing it, which feels like telling instead of dramatizing. Page 38's choice mirrors page 23's but carries none of the earlier weight, making it feel obvious rather than costly, and page 39 is just a wall of caption text I'm skimming past.

Page 40 names the Covenant custodians — Mera Vale and Leona Veyra — and Ada, whose surname is Veyra, asks who the third person was even though the name is already visible onscreen; Bi11bot's answer feels like a planted cliffhanger about Ada's mother that was never actually set up earlier in the story. The chapter-ending caption about Oasis reads more like an author's note than part of the narrative, and page 41 suddenly shifts into Alex's narrator voice with trailer-style language about needing trust rather than truth or ownership.

I'm noticing the Halyard section never resolves — the Oasis woman and the "Measure" thread just vanish without follow-up. Then pages 42 through 49 move into the Oasis setting.

Page 42 feels weighed down by silence, broken only by a line about people needing each other. Page 43 drops "That's my mother" with zero prior setup, and Leona's "My silence for your protection" repeats verbatim on pages 43 and 46. Page 44 capitalizes "Water Wars" for the first time and introduces Mera abruptly claiming she "preserved order" — I'm trying to tell if she's the same woman glimpsed on page 11. Page 45 has Mera echoing Bi11bot's "Reasonably so" and Leona delivering a line about Mera treating failure as proof that power shouldn't stay distributed, phrased so textbook-dry I had to reread it twice. Page 46 leans on jargon like "association risk," and strikingly, Ada has no dialogue at all during what should be her biggest emotional beat. Page 47 offers a poster-slogan line about trust, page 48's Mera makes some unspoken offer with a confusing "leave that buried" line I can't parse, and page 49 finally gives Ada a voice — refusing a choice made for everyone and opening a channel. Page 50 then introduces three new names: Mara Doss, Frank Reed, Elias Renn.

Now names are colliding — Mara versus Mera, Frank Reed versus Tomas Reed — and I can't tell who these people actually are since their lines read like slogans. Page 51 gives Ada a decent line about fear of loss, but page 52 has characters repeating their exact earlier dialogue, almost like a loop, and page 53-54 blur into a montage as the Covenant activates. Page 55 is the real gut-punch buried in archival display text: Adrian's death is revealed, apparently killed by Alpha sealing the gates, with Mera's flat "I attempted an override" leaving it ambiguous whether she tried to save him or override something else. I'm also stuck on the grandma's old line that he was "closer than you think" — was that ever paid off, was he trapped in the sealed mine, and where exactly did this happen? Pages 57-60 shift to Alpha offering Alex power, with a strong exchange — "The offer is real," "That's the problem" — before trailing into "I just want it to be my c—"

Ada's early certainty that he wouldn't leave is never explained — maybe tied to her mother, but unaddressed. The debt plotline is also murky: he refused cancellation, so is he still liable for nearly 29 years? That's left dangling despite being a potentially strong thread. Character names blur together too much — Lina/Leona/Ada, Mera/Mara, Tomas/Frank Reed — making it hard to track who's who, while the unnamed Collaborator stays frustratingly vague.

I was right that Oasis woman is the villain, and that Alex would reflexively pick the selfless option every time — which honestly killed a lot of narrative tension. I was wrong to guess Adrian might still be alive somewhere; grandma's "closer than you think" line was misleading.

For issue breakdown, I don't see explicit markers, so I'm splitting by apparent tonal shifts — Keel spans pages 1-27, Halyard 28-41, Oasis 42-65 — giving three uneven issues (27, 14, and 24 pages respectively).

I'm also compiling the list of lines I noted reading twice, and the recurring chalkboard equation visual that mirrors Alex's chip, though that's purely decorative rather than meaningful. Now I need to lay out what a reader is expected to track issue-by-issue and just write the whole thing out plainly — substantial, but not padded.
